title: Pneumonia, Aspiration & Tuberculosis: Infection Control, Oxygenation and Sepsis Prevention
html:
Pneumonia, aspiration lung injury, and pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) can all present with cough, dyspnea, fever, abnormal lung sounds, or infiltrates, yet their immediate hazards differ. The RN must stabilize gas exchange, identify deterioration, obtain useful specimens without delaying urgent treatment, apply transmission precautions based on the suspected organism, and prevent aspiration and hospital-acquired harm.

Learning goals

  • Recognize pneumonia severity and early respiratory failure or sepsis.
  • Coordinate cultures, imaging, oxygen, antimicrobials, fluids, and reassessment safely.
  • Differentiate aspiration pneumonitis from aspiration pneumonia at the bedside.
  • Initiate airborne precautions immediately when pulmonary TB is suspected.
  • Teach secretion clearance, aspiration prevention, TB adherence, and discharge warning signs.
  • Evaluate whether treatment is improving oxygenation, perfusion, function, and infection.

Assess oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion first

Begin with airway patency, respiratory rate and pattern, work of breathing, ability to speak, oxygen saturation, mental status, skin color, pulse, blood pressure, temperature, urine output, and overall appearance. Auscultate both lungs and assess cough, sputum, pleuritic pain, hydration, mobility, and baseline cardiopulmonary function. Position upright when tolerated and give oxygen to the prescribed target.

Escalate immediately for severe hypoxemia, increasing oxygen need, exhaustion, cyanosis, new confusion, hypotension, oliguria, mottling, inability to protect the airway, or rapidly rising work of breathing. Pulse oximetry does not measure ventilation; blood gases and advanced respiratory support may be needed when fatigue, hypercapnia, or severe illness is suspected.

Older adults may not present with a high fever
Acute confusion, weakness, falls, poor intake, tachypnea, or functional decline may be the first clues. Compare with baseline and search promptly for hypoxemia, infection, medication effects, and other causes.

Classify the setting and host

Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, and aspiration-associated pneumonia have different likely organisms and resistance risks. Review recent hospitalization and antibiotics, residence and exposures, swallowing or consciousness problems, immune status, structural lung disease, travel, vaccination, smoking, and local epidemiology. Do not select isolation or antibiotics from a label alone.

Bacterial and viral infections are common causes, and coinfection can occur. Sputum color alone cannot identify the organism or prove that antibiotics are required. The diagnosis integrates symptoms, examination, imaging, oxygenation, laboratory data, microbiology when indicated, and the response over time.

Cultures should be useful—not a source of dangerous delay

Obtain an adequate sputum specimen and blood cultures when ordered and clinically indicated, preferably before the first antimicrobial dose if this can occur promptly. Verify identity, use correct containers and technique, label at the bedside, and send specimens without delay. A saliva-contaminated sputum sample may mislead treatment.

Do not postpone time-sensitive antimicrobial therapy or resuscitation while waiting for a difficult specimen. Document collection time relative to medications. When results return, compare organism, susceptibilities, clinical response, allergies, renal and hepatic function, and local guidance so therapy can be narrowed, changed, or stopped appropriately.

Support gas exchange and secretion clearance

Use upright positioning, prescribed oxygen, hydration appropriate to the client's perfusion and cardiac or renal status, pain control that preserves ventilation, mobility, turning, coughing, and coached deep breathing. Incentive spirometry may support selected postoperative plans but does not replace mobilization, pain control, or treatment of infection.

Suction only when secretions cannot be cleared and use the least invasive effective approach. Bronchodilators are useful for coexisting bronchospasm, not as universal pneumonia therapy. Reassess breath sounds, cough effectiveness, oxygen need, work of breathing, mentation, temperature, intake and output, and activity tolerance after interventions.

Aspiration can cause chemical or infectious injury

Aspiration risk rises with dysphagia, stroke, impaired consciousness, vomiting, reflux, sedatives, seizures, weak cough, poor oral health, enteral feeding, and unsafe positioning. A witnessed aspiration may cause chemical pneumonitis from gastric contents; bacterial aspiration pneumonia may emerge with persistent or worsening infectious findings. Imaging cannot always distinguish them immediately, so the clinical course matters.

During active aspiration, stop oral or enteral intake, position to protect the airway, suction visible material as appropriate, provide oxygen, assess breathing and circulation, and call for rapid help if respiratory distress or airway compromise develops. Do not perform a blind finger sweep. Antibiotics are not automatically indicated for every chemical aspiration event; treatment follows the clinical assessment and authorized plan.

Prevent recurrent aspiration

Keep the head of bed elevated when appropriate, verify feeding-tube placement and prescribed feeding practices, pause feeding when safety requires, and assess for abdominal distention, vomiting, sedation, and respiratory change. Follow swallow-screen and speech-language pathology recommendations, prescribed texture and liquid consistency, upright feeding, small bites or sips, pacing, and supervision.

Provide regular oral care because oral bacterial burden contributes to pneumonia risk. Confirm that dentures and hearing or vision supports are available when they improve safe feeding. Teach caregivers to stop feeding and seek help for coughing, choking, a wet voice, breathlessness, or reduced alertness.

Suspected pulmonary TB requires airborne protection

Consider pulmonary TB with persistent cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, compatible imaging, exposure, birth or residence in a high-prevalence setting, congregate living, or immune compromise. Symptoms and risk vary; do not wait for confirmation before protecting others.

Place a client with suspected infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB in an airborne infection isolation room with the door closed and follow facility notification procedures. Staff use a fit-tested N95 or higher-level respirator before entry. Limit transport to essential purposes; when transport is necessary, place a surgical or procedure mask on the client if tolerated, notify the receiving area, and maintain respiratory hygiene.

Isolation is based on suspicion, not a positive test
Initiate airborne precautions promptly. Do not discontinue them because one smear is negative; follow the full diagnostic assessment, facility policy, infection prevention, and public-health guidance.

TB testing and treatment require coordination

Evaluation may include chest imaging, nucleic-acid amplification testing, acid-fast bacilli smears, cultures, and susceptibility testing. Sputum collection that can aerosolize organisms occurs in an appropriate isolation environment. A negative screening blood or skin test does not independently rule out active disease in a symptomatic client.

Active TB requires multidrug therapy selected and monitored by qualified clinicians with public-health coordination. Reinforce taking every dose exactly as directed and reporting adverse effects promptly. Depending on the regimen, assess for jaundice, dark urine, persistent nausea, abdominal pain, neuropathy, visual change, rash, fever, or hearing problems. Never tell a client to stop or restart drugs independently unless an emergency instruction or authorized plan directs it.

Latent TB infection means organisms are present without clinical disease and the person is not contagious; active pulmonary or laryngeal TB may be infectious. Avoid stigmatizing language, protect privacy, use qualified interpretation, and explain the reason for isolation and follow-up.

Pneumonia can become sepsis and organ failure

Trend for infection plus new organ dysfunction: altered mentation, worsening oxygenation, hypotension, cool or mottled skin, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, rising lactate, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, or hepatic or renal change. Fever may be absent. Activate the sepsis pathway promptly when the pattern is concerning.

Obtain ordered cultures and lactate, administer antimicrobials and individualized fluids promptly, monitor response, and prepare vasopressor or critical-care support when shock persists. Fluids require repeated evaluation—especially with heart failure or kidney disease—using blood pressure, perfusion, lung findings, urine output, and other ordered measures.

Watch for local and respiratory complications

Failure to improve may signal resistant or incorrect therapy, empyema, parapneumonic effusion, abscess, obstruction, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, malignancy, or a noninfectious mimic. Increasing unilateral pain, dullness, persistent fever, toxicity, or oxygen need warrants reassessment and possible repeat imaging or drainage evaluation.

Severe inflammation can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome. Worsening bilateral opacities, refractory hypoxemia, and escalating support require critical-care management. Do not normalize increasing oxygen needs as an expected part of recovery.

Prevent hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated harm

Perform hand hygiene, use transmission-based precautions appropriate to the pathogen, clean shared equipment, and remove unnecessary invasive devices. For ventilated clients, follow the local evidence-based bundle: head-of-bed elevation when not contraindicated, regular oral care, daily assessment of sedation and ventilator liberation readiness, aspiration-risk reduction, and appropriate subglottic secretion management when available.

Do not routinely break ventilator circuits or replace components without indication. Use aseptic technique for airway care, evaluate cuff and tube security within role and policy, and coordinate mobility and spontaneous awakening or breathing processes with the team.

Discharge teaching prevents return

Reconcile antibiotics and other respiratory medicines, verify duration and timing, review adverse effects, and use teach-back. Address smoking cessation, recommended vaccination, nutrition, hydration when appropriate, gradual activity, oral care, cough hygiene, and follow-up. TB discharge requires public-health and infection-control coordination before the client leaves.

Seek urgent help for severe breathlessness, blue or gray color, new confusion, syncope, chest pain, hemoptysis, inability to keep fluids or medicines down, falling oxygen saturation below the individualized plan, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Explain that cough and fatigue may resolve gradually, but the overall trajectory should improve.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Collect respiratory effort, oxygenation, mentation, perfusion, temperature, cough and sputum, aspiration risk, TB exposure, imaging, microbiology, recent care, and baseline function.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish stable infection from respiratory failure or sepsis, chemical aspiration from evolving bacterial infection, and routine pneumonia precautions from suspected airborne TB.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Airway compromise, severe hypoxemia, shock, inability to protect the airway, and uncontained suspected TB are immediate threats.
  4. Generate solutions: Position, oxygenate, isolate correctly, obtain useful specimens, administer authorized therapy, support clearance and perfusion, and reduce aspiration risk.
  5. Take action: Escalate deterioration, begin indicated precautions before confirmation, avoid treatment delays, and coordinate respiratory, infectious-disease, swallowing, pharmacy, and public-health expertise.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend oxygen need, work of breathing, mentation, hemodynamics, urine output, temperature, laboratory and imaging findings, mobility, intake, tolerance, and teach-back.

Clinical example

An older adult admitted after vomiting becomes confused, tachypneic, hypoxemic, and hypotensive. The RN stops oral intake, positions the client upright, applies oxygen, assesses airway protection and lung findings, activates urgent evaluation for aspiration-related lung injury and sepsis, obtains ordered cultures without delaying therapy, and reassesses perfusion and respiratory response. If a separate history reveals prolonged cough, weight loss, and TB exposure, airborne precautions begin immediately while diagnostic testing proceeds.
